questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'At nine o'clock last night we ___ dinner when the power went out.'
questions.context: A witness describes what was happening when the accident occurred.

options.text: were having
options.feedback: Correct. 'Were having' is the past continuous, which marks the longer action that was already under way when the second event happened.

options.text: are having
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are having' is present continuous, which places the dinner at the current moment instead of last night.

options.text: had
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Had' would require a past participle after it and describes an earlier completed state, not an ongoing dinner.

options.text: have
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have' is the base form and cannot carry the past progressive meaning on its own.

questions.explanation:
The structure 'was or were plus verb-ing' expresses an action in progress in the past, which is exactly what an interrupted dinner is.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct past continuous form of the verb 'to sleep'.
questions.context: A friend describes a scene from a film.

options.text: slept
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Slept' is the past simple, which marks a completed action rather than an ongoing one.

options.text: was sleeping
options.feedback: Correct. The singular subject takes 'was' plus the gerund, giving the past continuous form 'was sleeping'.

options.text: were sleeping
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were' is the plural auxiliary and does not agree with a singular subject such as 'he'.

options.text: sleep
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Sleep' is the base form and cannot express any tense without an auxiliary.

questions.explanation:
The past continuous always pairs was or were with the gerund, and the auxiliary must agree in number with the subject.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the past continuous marks the shorter, backgrounded action.
questions.context: A detective reconstructs an interrupted conversation.

options.text: I rang when the phone was ringing.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I rang' in the main clause would make the call the long background action, which is not the situation described.

options.text: I was ringing when the phone rang.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I was ringing' makes the call the background action and the phone the interruption, which reverses the narrative.

options.text: I was cooking when the phone rang.
options.feedback: Correct. Cooking is the longer action already in progress, so it takes the past continuous while the call is the interruption.

options.text: I rang when I rang the phone.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I rang when I rang the phone' repeats the same action and cannot express an interruption.

questions.explanation:
The action that is presented as already under way takes the past continuous; the shorter action that cuts into it takes the past simple.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'While my sister ___ the guitar, my brother was doing his homework.'
questions.context: A student compares two things happening at the same past moment.

options.text: has playing
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has playing' lacks a past participle after 'has' and is not a valid form.

options.text: plays
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Plays' is present tense and cannot share a past time frame with 'was doing'.

options.text: played
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Played' in the while-clause would make the two actions sequential rather than simultaneous.

options.text: was playing
options.feedback: Correct. Two simultaneous past actions, both in progress, take the past continuous with matching was or were forms.

questions.explanation:
When two past actions run at the same time, English uses the past continuous for both, which makes the simultaneity explicit.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct negative past continuous sentence.
questions.context: A negative past continuous is needed in a description.

options.text: She wasn't sleeping at eleven.
options.feedback: Correct. Negating the auxiliary with 'was not' plus the gerund produces the negative past continuous, contracted to 'wasn't'.

options.text: She not was sleeping at eleven.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Not' cannot precede the auxiliary in standard English word order.

options.text: She wasn't sleep at eleven.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Wasn't sleep' lacks the gerund; after the auxiliary the verb must appear as 'sleeping'.

options.text: She didn't sleep at eleven.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Didn't sleep' is a negative past simple and would describe a single completed action rather than an ongoing one.

questions.explanation:
Negation in the continuous is formed on the auxiliary, not on the gerund, which is why 'wasn't sleeping' is the correct structure.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct past continuous question.
questions.context: A teacher asks about a scene in a photograph.

options.text: What did you do at that moment?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Did you do' asks about a single completed action, not about what was in progress.

options.text: What were you doing at that moment?
options.feedback: Correct. A question in the past continuous inverts the auxiliary to the front and keeps the gerund after the subject.

options.text: What was you doing at that moment?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was' cannot be used with the subject 'you'; the plural auxiliary 'were' is required.

options.text: What you were doing at that moment?
options.feedback: Wrong. Without the auxiliary at the front there is no question structure, so this is not a well-formed question.

questions.explanation:
The plural auxiliary 'were' is obligatory with 'you', and it must be inverted to the front of the question.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses two past continuous clauses for simultaneous states.
questions.context: A report links two background states in the past.

options.text: The lights were flickering and the room froze.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Froze' is past simple and presents the cold as a completed change rather than a continuing condition.

options.text: The lights flickered and the room was freezing.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Flickered' in the simple past suggests the flickering came to an end, which a state description should not do.

options.text: The lights were flickering and the room was freezing.
options.feedback: Correct. Describing two ongoing states at the same moment requires the past continuous in both clauses.

options.text: The lights flickered and the room froze.
options.feedback: Wrong. Two past simple clauses give a sequence of finished events instead of a simultaneous shared scene.

questions.explanation:
Shared scenes in narration are best rendered with the past continuous, because it presents the situation as a single moment rather than a chain of events.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly marks the action in progress in the past and the habit with the past simple.
questions.context: An interview distinguishes an action from a habit.

options.text: At that moment he smokes, although he avoided cigarettes.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Smokes' is present tense, which cannot sit in a sentence narrated from a past viewpoint.

options.text: At that moment he was smoking, although he usually was avoiding cigarettes.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Usually was avoiding' misplaces the adverb before the auxiliary and assigns a continuous to a habit.

options.text: At that moment he smoked, although he was usually avoiding cigarettes.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'He smoked' would place the action at a completed past moment and 'was usually avoiding' describes an ongoing state, inverting both roles.

options.text: At that moment he was smoking, although he usually avoided cigarettes.
options.feedback: Correct. The specific ongoing action uses the past continuous while 'usually' plus the past simple presents the general habit.

questions.explanation:
The same contrast that separates the present simple from the present continuous also operates in the past, since English marks duration rather than time of narration.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly joins two past continuous clauses with 'while'.
questions.context: A novelist describes a parallel background action.

options.text: While the rain was pouring, the children were playing in the yard.
options.feedback: Correct. Both clauses use the past continuous, which is the standard way to present two simultaneous past actions.

options.text: While the rain was pouring, the children were play in the yard.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were play' lacks the gerund after the plural auxiliary.

options.text: While the rain was pouring, the children played in the yard.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Played' in the main clause would present the children as finishing their play rather than continuing it.

options.text: While the rain poured, the children were playing in the yard.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Rain poured' in the past simple suggests a completed downpour rather than an action continuing.

questions.explanation:
The while-clause and the main clause should share the same past frame when both actions overlap in time.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'I ___ for a scholarship last March, so I missed the deadline.'
questions.context: A job application mentions a task in progress at a past deadline.

options.text: applied
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Applied' is the past simple and would present the application as a single completed event.

options.text: was applying
options.feedback: Correct. An application under way at a stated past moment takes the past continuous to show it was still running.

options.text: am applying
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Am applying' is present continuous, which has no connection to last March.

options.text: apply
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Apply' is the base form and cannot convey a past situation without an auxiliary.

questions.explanation:
The past continuous is the form that marks an activity as still in progress at a specific past reference point.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly describes an action in progress at a precise past moment.
questions.context: A traveller tells what was happening at a past moment.

options.text: At noon we have waited at the airport.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have waited' is the present perfect, which cannot be placed with a finished past time such as noon.

options.text: At noon we waited at the airport.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Waited' is the past simple and suggests the waiting completed at noon rather than continuing.

options.text: At noon we were waiting at the airport.
options.feedback: Correct. A precise past moment with an activity that was still ongoing is best expressed with the past continuous.

options.text: At noon we are waiting at the airport.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are waiting' is present continuous and belongs to the current moment rather than to a past period.

questions.explanation:
A specific past clock time is the classic trigger for the past continuous because it locates an action inside that moment.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which 'while' correctly introduces the longer background action.
questions.context: A grammar task compares the past simple and the past continuous with 'while'.

options.text: While she is revising her notes, the bell rang.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is revising' is present continuous and cannot serve as the background of a past simple event.

options.text: While she was revising her notes, the bell rang already.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Rang already' adds an adverb that conflicts with the simple past form and does not repair the meaning.

options.text: While she revised her notes, the bell was ringing.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The bell was ringing' makes the bell the background, but a short sound is better presented as an interruption.

options.text: While she was revising her notes, the bell rang.
options.feedback: Correct. Revision is the longer ongoing activity and the bell is the brief interrupting event, which is the standard past continuous plus past simple pattern.

questions.explanation:
Which action takes the continuous depends on which one lasted longer, not on which clause appears first in the sentence.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly describes a longer activity extending up to a past point.
questions.context: A historian notes what had been happening before a decision.

options.text: They had been working on the project for months before the funding stopped.
options.feedback: Correct. A duration extending up to a past point requires the past perfect continuous, since the activity outlasted the earlier reference moment.

options.text: They worked on the project for months before the funding stopped.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Worked' is the past simple and would express a single bounded action rather than an extended duration.

options.text: They have been working on the project for months before the funding stopped.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have been working' is the present perfect continuous and belongs to the present, not to a past reference point.

options.text: They were working on the project for months before the funding stopped.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were working' marks an action in progress but not one that continued right up to the earlier past moment.

questions.explanation:
English reserves the perfect continuous for durations that lead up to a past moment, and that is precisely the situation described here.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct short answer to the question 'Were you revising at nine?'
questions.context: A classmate asks about an ongoing activity from a past point of view.

options.text: No, I didn't.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Didn't' is the past simple auxiliary and answers a different question about a completed action.

options.text: No, I wasn't.
options.feedback: Correct. A negative short answer to a past continuous question repeats the auxiliary 'was' with 'not' and omits the gerund.

options.text: No, I not revising.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Not' cannot stand alone in a short answer, and the gerund form is wrong after 'was'.

options.text: No, I wasn't revise.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'I wasn't revise' lacks the gerund; a short answer contains only the pronoun and the auxiliary.

questions.explanation:
Short answers consist of a pronoun plus the auxiliary, so a negative reply to a past continuous question must use 'wasn't'.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the past continuous and the past simple are used in a way that creates an illogical overlap.
questions.context: A reviewer points out an inconsistency in a student's narrative.

options.text: He was driving home while he realised he had left his wallet at the office.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'While he realised' sets the realisation as background rather than as the moment of interruption, which weakens the sequence.

options.text: He was driving home when he realised he leaves his wallet at the office.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'He realises' is present tense, which clashes with the past narration and is the inconsistency the reviewer is flagging.

options.text: He was driving home when he realised he had left his wallet at the office.
options.feedback: Correct. 'He was driving' is a valid ongoing past action but 'he realises' is present tense and cannot form the interrupting clause.

options.text: He drives home when he realised he had left his wallet at the office.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'He drives home' is present tense and cannot belong to a sentence anchored in the past.

questions.explanation:
A narrative built on the past requires consistency: an interrupting event in such a sentence must be expressed with the past simple.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly describes movement that continued inside a limited area at a past moment.
questions.context: An athlete describes a specific instant of movement.

options.text: He was run up and down the court when the whistle blew.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was run' uses the base form after the auxiliary, which is only correct with a participle.

options.text: He runs up and down the court when the whistle blew.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Runs' is present tense and cannot be coordinated with a past interruption.

options.text: He ran up and down the court when the whistle blew.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Ran' presents the movement as completed before the whistle, which removes the sense of activity at that instant.

options.text: He was running up and down the court when the whistle blew.
options.feedback: Correct. Movement contained within a limited area and still in progress takes the past continuous.

questions.explanation:
Verbs of movement restricted by an adverb such as 'up and down' are conventionally tested with the continuous because the movement is ongoing.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly contrasts an action under way with a single repeated event inside a past period.
questions.context: A linguistic exercise examines a subtle difference in aspect.

options.text: He was cycling to school every day that week.
options.feedback: Correct. The continuous with a repeated adverb phrase presents each instance as an unfinished process within the period.

options.text: He has cycled to school every day that week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has cycled' is the present perfect and cannot be used with the closed past phrase 'that week'.

options.text: He was cycling to school once that week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Once' would be incompatible with a continuous, since a single completed trip is better rendered with the simple past.

options.text: He cycled to school every day that week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Cycled' presents the cycling as a series of completed events, which is the habitual reading of that phrase.

questions.explanation:
Continuous aspect with a repeated phrase inside a past period changes the reading from discrete completed events to processes that were individually under way.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct version of the sentence the editor accepts.
questions.context: An editing task corrects an aspect error in a travel narrative.

options.text: We were driving along the coast when the engine makes a strange noise.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Makes' is present tense and breaks the past frame established by 'were driving'.

options.text: We were driving along the coast when the engine started making a strange noise.
options.feedback: Correct. The journey is background and ongoing, while the engine noise is the short event that interrupted it, both anchored in the past.

options.text: We drive along the coast when the engine started making a strange noise.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Drive' is present tense and contradicts 'started making' in the same clause.

options.text: We drove along the coast while the engine was making a strange noise.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'While' turns the engine noise into a longer background action rather than the interruption.

questions.explanation:
The editing task tests whether the learner can keep the aspect distinction consistent within a single past narration.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement correctly explains why the second sentence is preferred in formal writing?
questions.context: A comparison of two sentences is the object of the task.

options.text: 'The committee debated the proposal' is less accurate because the past simple cannot describe completed actions.
options.feedback: Wrong. The past simple describes completed actions perfectly well, so the claim in this option is false.

options.text: 'The committee was debating the proposal' is preferred because the continuous is always more formal than the simple past.
options.feedback: Wrong. The continuous is not uniformly more formal; register plays a separate role and this explanation is inaccurate.

options.text: 'The committee was debating the proposal' presents the discussion as an ongoing process, which suits a description of a stage in a long process.
options.feedback: Correct. This explains the aspectual difference rather than asserting a blanket rule, and it correctly identifies what the continuous contributes.

options.text: 'The committee was debating the proposal' is preferred because English has no simple past form of the verb to debate.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Debate' has a regular simple past form, so the claim that no such form exists is incorrect.

questions.explanation:
A strong statement of preference rests on the meaning of the forms involved, not on a false generalisation about register or existence of inflections.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly avoids the past continuous with a state verb.
questions.context: An exam item tests the negative past continuous with stative verbs.

options.text: She not know the answer at that point.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Not' cannot precede the base form without an auxiliary and 'know' would also be the wrong tense.

options.text: She didn't knew the answer at that point.
options.feedback: Wrong. After 'did' the verb must be the base form, so 'knew' cannot follow it.

options.text: She wasn't knowing the answer at that point.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Wasn't knowing' is ungrammatical; stative verbs generally resist the progressive form.

options.text: She didn't know the answer at that point.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Know' is a stative verb, so standard English uses the simple past and does not allow the progressive in this sense.

questions.explanation: The restriction on the progressive with stative verbs is one of the most frequently tested points in English grammar examinations.
